title: Multilingual P2P Software: Driving Procurement Adoption Among Non-English Speaking Staff in Southeast Asia
summary: P2P rollouts in Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia stall when staff can't use English. See how local-language UI and multilingual OCR lift adoption.
body_markdown:
**TL;DR:** Procure-to-pay systems succeed or fail on requester adoption, and in Thailand, Vietnam and Indonesia many requesters and approvers are not comfortable working in English. A multilingual P2P platform with a native local-language interface, automatic language defaults by location and AI invoice capture that reads Thai, Vietnamese, Bahasa and Chinese removes the most common reason staff work around the system. Language support should be tested with real local documents during vendor selection, not assumed.


## The Adoption Problem Hiding in Regional P2P Rollouts


When regional finance teams plan a P2P rollout, they focus on approval matrices, ERP integration and tax. Language is often treated as a footnote. That is a mistake, because P2P is one of the few finance systems used mostly by people outside finance.


In a recent discovery session, a finance analyst at a manufacturing and distribution group with subsidiaries in Thailand, Malaysia, Singapore, Vietnam and Indonesia raised it directly. Their staff, especially in Thailand and Vietnam, might not be very familiar with English. UI translation would be great, he said, though he framed it as a good-to-have because browser translation exists.


That framing is common, and understandable from a finance perspective. But consider who uses a P2P system:


- **Requesters** in operations, warehouses, sales and admin, raising purchase requests
- **Approvers** such as department and country heads, often approving on mobile
- **Receivers** confirming deliveries
- **Finance** , a small minority of users


In that group, Thailand was described as the main battlefield, with the most staff. If the largest user base cannot comfortably use the system, adoption suffers exactly where it matters most. The[EF English Proficiency Index](https://www.ef.com/wwen/epi/) has consistently placed several Southeast Asian markets, including Thailand, in lower proficiency bands, which matches what finance teams see on the ground.


## What Happens When Requesters Can’t Use the System


Language friction does not show up as a complaint. It shows up as behaviour:


Behaviour Root cause Impact on P2P


Requesters ask finance to raise PRs for them Unfamiliar interface terms Finance becomes a data entry team


Purchases made first, PR raised later Process feels hard, so it is skipped Spend control lost, after-the-fact POs


Wrong cost centre or category selected Labels misunderstood Misallocated costs, rework at month end


Approvals delayed Approvers unsure what they are approving Longer PR-to-PO cycle


Comments written in local language in English fields No local-language support Audit trail hard to read


Each of these undermines the reason for buying a P2P system: controlling spend before it happens. Our article on[PR and GRN procurement process inefficiencies](https://peakflo.co/blog/pr-grn-procurement-process-inefficiencies) shows how quickly informal workarounds grow once they start.


## Why Browser Translation Is Not Enough


Browser translation is a reasonable fallback, but it has real limits for a business system:


- **Inconsistent terms.** “Purchase request” may be translated differently on different screens.
- **Emails and PDFs are not translated.** Approval emails, PO documents and notifications stay in English.
- **Mobile apps are not covered.** Many approvers act from their phone.
- **Layouts break.** Longer translated strings overflow buttons and tables.
- **Dropdown values may be mistranslated** , such as cost centre or category names.


A native multilingual interface uses a controlled vocabulary, so a Thai requester sees the same term for “cost centre” on the PR form, the approval email and the mobile app.


## The Two Halves of Multilingual P2P


Multilingual P2P has two distinct parts, and both matter.


### 1. A local-language user interface


The screens, emails and mobile views that requesters and approvers use. The best platforms set the default language automatically. Peakflo, for example, uses the location of the user logging in: someone in Bangkok sees Thai, someone in Kuala Lumpur sees Bahasa Melayu, someone in Jakarta sees Bahasa Indonesia. Users can switch at any time.


### 2. Multilingual document capture


Suppliers in the region send invoices, quotations and delivery orders in local languages and scripts:[Thai script](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thai_script) ,[Vietnamese with diacritics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnamese_alphabet) , Bahasa, Chinese characters, often mixed with English on the same line.[Optical character recognition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Optical_character_recognition) designed for English struggles with these. Modern AI extraction handles them.


During the same discovery demo, the analyst’s reaction to seeing AI capture multiple languages written on the same invoice line was that it was mind-blowing. That reaction is common, because legacy OCR in the region often fails exactly here, forcing AP teams to retype local-language invoices.


Capability Legacy approach Multilingual P2P


Interface language English only, or browser translation Native Thai, Vietnamese, Bahasa, Chinese, English


Default language Manual per user Automatic by location or entity


Approval emails English Local language with configurable fields


Invoice capture English-trained OCR, manual retyping AI extraction across dozens of languages, including mixed-language lines


Handwritten documents Manual entry AI extraction with human review on exceptions


Data posted to ERP Same Same, language does not change GL or supplier data


## Language and the ERP: What Changes and What Doesn’t


Finance leaders sometimes worry that a multilingual interface will create inconsistent data. It does not. Interface language changes labels, not values. A requester in Hanoi and one in Singapore pick from the same cost centres, suppliers and GL codes. The ERP posting is identical.


What does help is agreeing terminology across countries before go-live. Decide the local-language term for PR, PO, GRN, cost centre and approval policy once, and use it everywhere. This matters for audit too:[segregation of duties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_duties) evidence is only useful if reviewers can read it.


## Training and Change Management in Local Languages


Language support in the software is half of adoption. The other half is how you introduce it. The[Prosci ADKAR model](https://www.prosci.com/methodology/adkar) is a useful lens: awareness, desire, knowledge, ability and reinforcement. Language barriers hit knowledge and ability hardest.


Practical steps that work in Southeast Asian rollouts:


1. **Train by role, not by module.** A requester needs to raise a PR and check status. An approver needs to approve from email or mobile. Keep each session to those tasks.
2. **Run sessions in the local language.** Use local super-users in each country.
3. **Lead with mobile and email.** Approvers who can approve from a daily email in their language rarely need training at all.
4. **Use short local-language quick guides** instead of long English manuals.
5. **Reinforce with data.** Share PR compliance by department each month.


The table below shows a simple adoption scorecard.


Metric Why it matters Healthy target after 90 days


Spend through approved PRs Core control coverage Most addressable spend


PRs raised by requesters, not finance Self-service adoption Large majority


Median PR approval time Approver engagement Within one to two working days


PRs rejected for missing or wrong data Interface clarity Falling month on month


Invoices with no PO found at AP Off-system purchasing Falling month on month


## Choosing a Multilingual P2P Vendor: A Checklist


When evaluating vendors, test language with real documents, not slides:


- Upload real supplier invoices from each country, including Thai, Vietnamese and mixed-language ones
- Check approval emails and the mobile app in each language, not just the web interface
- Ask how the default language is set and whether users can switch
- Confirm that dropdown values such as cost centres can carry local-language descriptions
- Check handwritten and stamped documents, which are common in regional supply chains
- Confirm that GL, tax and supplier data remain consistent across languages


A good vendor will also understand the regional compliance landscape. Our guide to[GST, VAT and SST in procure-to-pay across Southeast Asia](https://peakflo.co/blog/southeast-asia-gst-vat-sst-procure-to-pay-tax-configuration) covers the tax side.

## Our Verdict: Is Multilingual Support a Must-Have?


### Treat it as a must-have if


- A large share of requesters and approvers work in Thai, Vietnamese or Bahasa
- Your largest user population is in a market with lower English proficiency
- Suppliers send invoices and delivery orders in local languages
- Approvers act mainly from mobile


### It can be a nice-to-have if


- Users are mostly finance staff working in English
- Your P2P scope is limited to a single English-speaking entity
- Suppliers invoice in English


**Our Recommendation:** For regional rollouts, weigh language support heavily for requester and approver adoption, and test multilingual invoice capture with real documents. The cost of poor adoption, spend bypassing the system, is far higher than the effort of choosing a vendor that speaks your users’ languages.


## Conclusion


A P2P system is only as good as the share of spend that goes through it. In Southeast Asia, that depends on whether a warehouse supervisor in Thailand or a department head in Vietnam can raise and approve requests without struggling with English.


A native multilingual interface, automatic language defaults and AI capture that reads local documents turn language from a barrier into a non-issue. Combined with simple[approval workflow automation](https://peakflo.co/accounts-payable/approval-workflow-automation) , they make P2P a system people actually use.


## Frequently Asked Questions


### Why does language matter in P2P software adoption?


Most P2P users are not finance staff. They are requesters and approvers in operations, sales and warehouses. If they cannot comfortably read the interface, they avoid raising purchase requests, fill fields incorrectly or ask finance to do it for them, which defeats the purpose of the system.


### Is browser translation enough for a P2P system?


Browser translation is a useful fallback but it translates labels inconsistently, can break layouts and does not translate emails, PDFs or mobile apps. A native local-language interface gives consistent terminology across every screen, notification and approval email.


### Which languages should a Southeast Asian P2P platform support?


At minimum Thai, Vietnamese, Bahasa Indonesia, Bahasa Melayu and English, with Simplified and Traditional Chinese for groups with Greater China headquarters. Invoice capture should also read these languages, including mixed-language documents.


### What is multilingual OCR?


Multilingual OCR is document extraction that reads invoices, quotations and delivery orders written in several languages and scripts, such as Thai, Vietnamese with diacritics or Chinese characters, and converts them into structured fields for matching and posting.


### Can AI read invoices with two languages on the same line?


Yes. Modern AI extraction models can read mixed-language invoices where item descriptions combine, for example, Thai and English or Chinese and English on the same line, and still map them to the right PO lines.


### How can the interface language be set automatically?


Some platforms set the default language from the user’s location or IP address, so a user logging in from Bangkok sees Thai, from Kuala Lumpur sees Bahasa Melayu and from Jakarta sees Bahasa Indonesia. Users can still switch language manually.


### Does a multilingual UI affect the data posted to the ERP?


No. The interface language changes what users see, not the underlying data. GL codes, supplier IDs, cost centres and amounts remain identical, so finance reports and ERP postings stay consistent regardless of the language a requester used.


### How do you train non-English speaking users on a new P2P system?


Run role-based training in the local language, focused on the two or three tasks each role performs, such as raising a PR or approving from email. Short local-language guides and mobile-first workflows reduce training time more than long English manuals.


### What adoption metrics should we track after rollout?


Track the share of spend going through approved purchase requests, PRs raised by requesters rather than finance, approval turnaround time, rejected PRs due to missing data and off-system purchases discovered at invoice stage.


### Is UI translation a must-have or nice-to-have?


For finance users it is often a nice-to-have. For requesters and approvers in markets like Thailand and Vietnam it is frequently the difference between a system people use and one they work around, so it should weigh heavily in vendor selection for regional rollouts.
